request.task: A team of 6 engineers is starting a new B2B SaaS product. Should they use a monorepo or separate repositories? Give a recommendation.

final.final_answer:
Recommendation: start with a monorepo (with clear internal boundaries) for a 6-engineer team building a new B2B SaaS product.

Why this is the better default early on:
- You'll change APIs, data models, and shared libraries frequently; a monorepo makes cross-cutting refactors (backend + frontend + infra) atomic and reviewable.
- It reduces coordination tax: one issue/PR can update multiple components without version pinning or publish/release choreography between repos.
- Consistent tooling (lint/test/build, CI conventions, dependency management, security scanning) is easier to standardize in one place.
- Onboarding is simpler: one checkout, one set of scripts, one place to find code.

How to do it so it doesn't turn into a mess:
- Create a small set of top-level packages/apps (e.g., /apps/web, /apps/api, /packages/shared, /infra) and enforce ownership with CODEOWNERS.
- Use a build system that supports caching and "affected" builds/tests (e.g., Nx/Turborepo/Bazel/Gradle, depending on stack) so CI doesn't run everything on every change.
- Keep deployables independently deployable even inside the monorepo (separate pipelines per service/app; don't require "big bang" releases).
- Establish boundaries: avoid deep import chains; treat shared code as versioned packages within the monorepo (even if not published externally).

When separate repos become the better choice:
- Strongly different stacks with minimal shared code and few cross-cutting changes.
- Organizational scaling (many teams) where repo-level access control/compliance boundaries are required.
- You need fully independent lifecycles with very different release cadences and ownership, and monorepo tooling/CI can't keep up.

Pragmatic rule: start monorepo now, and split later only if the costs become obvious (CI time, access-control needs, or team/ownership scale). Splitting later is usually easier than trying to coordinate many repos during the rapid-change phase of a new product.
final.label: unanimous
caveats: This recommendation assumes the 6 engineers are working on a fairly unified, tightly-coupled product (shared APIs, data models, and frequent cross-cutting changes) — the typical situation for a new B2B SaaS build.

Read as: 'one product, one team, early-stage, high change velocity' — if you meant a scenario with strongly divergent tech stacks, separate compliance/access-control boundaries, or planned independent release cadences per component, the answer changes to separate repositories.

No dissent survived deliberation — all models converged on monorepo as the starting point; the only live variable is whether the team's actual situation matches the assumptions above (shared codebase, unified team) rather than a multi-team or multi-stack setup.

payload.answer: For a team of 6 engineers starting a new B2B SaaS product, I recommend starting with a monorepo. This approach centralizes all code for the frontend, backend, shared libraries, infrastructure-as-code, and tooling in a single repository. It simplifies dependency management, enforces consistent tooling and standards from day one, and makes it easier to implement cross-cutting changes and refactorings as the product evolves rapidly in its early stages. With a team of only 6, the coordination overhead of a monorepo is manageable, and modern tooling (like Turborepo, Nx, or pnpm workspaces) can handle build and test orchestration effectively. The primary risk—repository size and build times—is minimal at the start and can be mitigated with good tooling as the project grows. If, in the future, clear, independently deployable services with distinct lifecycles emerge, the team can consider splitting into a polyrepo setup, but beginning unified is the simpler, more productive default.

A team of 6 can manage the coordination overhead of a monorepo without significant tooling friction.
Modern monorepo tooling (e.g., Turborepo, Nx) effectively handles build and test orchestration for small to medium projects.
Starting with a monorepo enforces consistent tooling and standards across the codebase from the beginning.
The risk of repository bloat and slow build times is minimal for a new project and can be addressed later.
A monorepo is easier to split into polyrepos later than it is to merge separate repos into a monorepo.
assumptions: The B2B SaaS product will consist of multiple logical components (e.g., frontend, backend API, shared libraries, deployment configs).
The team intends to move quickly and iterate on the product, requiring frequent cross-component changes.
The team has the technical capability to set up and use modern monorepo tooling.
The product is starting from scratch, with no legacy code or pre-existing repository structure constraints.
The team size (6) is expected to remain stable in the near term, and all engineers will work across the full stack or multiple components.
The primary goal is development velocity and cohesion, not independent, decoupled deployment of services from day one.
payload.expected_consensus: Most other capable models will likely also recommend a monorepo for this scenario, emphasizing benefits like simplified dependency management, unified tooling, and ease of refactoring for a small, co-located team starting a new product. Some may caution about long-term scaling issues but will conclude that starting with a monorepo is the pragmatic choice.

The team should use a monorepo.

With only six engineers and a single new B2B SaaS product, the overhead of managing multiple repositories (CI/CD pipelines, dependency versioning, cross-repo coordination, onboarding) outweighs any perceived benefits of separation. A monorepo simplifies code sharing, ensures atomic changes across services or layers, streamlines testing and deployment, and reduces context-switching costs—all critical for a small, co-located team moving quickly in early-stage development. As the product and team scale significantly (e.g., dozens of microservices or >20 engineers), they can reconsider splitting, but starting with a monorepo is the pragmatic choice.
